questions.q: Which of the following is a well-formed runbook trigger condition?
options: "Checkout is slow"
"CheckoutLatencyP99 alert fires (>2s for 5 min)"
"Something is probably wrong with checkout"
"Users are complaining on social media"
questions.explain: A trigger condition should name the exact alert and threshold, not a vague symptom — this is what lets a responder confirm immediately whether this runbook applies.

questions.q: What makes a set of remediation steps like 'check if the database is the problem, and fix it if so' a poor runbook entry?
options: It's too long for an on-call engineer to read quickly
It lacks the specificity to actually follow under stress — it's a to-do item disguised as a procedure
It doesn't mention an escalation path
It should be written in a ticketing system instead of a runbook
questions.explain: A runbook needs concrete, specific steps — the actual query, command, or dashboard — not a restatement of the problem. Vague instructions fail the '3am test.'

questions.q: What is the key difference between auto-remediation and ChatOps?
options: Auto-remediation always requires more engineering effort to build than ChatOps
Auto-remediation takes action with no human in the loop; ChatOps keeps a human approving the action but removes the friction of switching tools
ChatOps is only used for SEV3 and SEV4 incidents
There is no meaningful difference — they are two names for the same pattern
questions.explain: Auto-remediation is fully automatic and best for low-risk, reversible fixes. ChatOps still requires human judgment but runs the command from a shared chat tool so the action and result are visible to the whole incident channel.

questions.q: Why is resizing a database connection pool better suited to a ChatOps command than full auto-remediation?
options: Because pool resizing is too complex for any script to execute
Because it has downstream cost and risk implications that warrant human approval, even though running the command itself should be low-friction
Because ChatOps commands are always faster than scripts
Because connection pools cannot be resized programmatically
questions.explain: Pool sizing affects cost and risk in ways that justify keeping a human in the loop for approval, while ChatOps still avoids the friction of switching tools mid-incident.

questions.q: What is the practical test for whether a runbook is good enough?
options: Whether it was reviewed by a manager
Whether a competent engineer unfamiliar with the specific service could follow it successfully at 3am
Whether it is shorter than one page
Whether it has been run successfully at least once before
questions.explain: The lesson's test for a good runbook is whether someone without deep familiarity with that specific service could execute it successfully under stress — if not, it needs more specificity.
